Revised assessment incorporating SLOOS insights:
The FOMC’s November 5, 2020 statement remains appropriately cautious and policy-supportive (near-zero rates, explicit outcome-based forward guidance, ongoing Treasury/MBS purchases). The Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey for Q3 2020 adds that, despite accommodative market conditions, bank credit supply is still restrictive: on net, banks tightened lending standards and terms for C&I and CRE loans and reported weaker demand; for households, standards tightened across residential mortgage categories and tightened alongside weaker demand for credit cards and auto loans. Respondents cited an uncertain economic outlook, reduced risk tolerance, and concerns over borrowers’ collateral and income. Many institutions also relied on forbearance/loan modification, which supports near-term credit performance but could mask underlying credit risk if the recovery falters.

Relative to the Financial Stability Report’s “elevated vulnerabilities” (high business leverage, CRE stress, nonbank fragilities), the SLOOS points to a continued headwind from the bank-intermediated credit channel, especially for businesses and CRE, and some consumer segments. Mitigants remain: strong bank capital/liquidity, improved funding conditions, and the Fed’s asset purchases and facilities that compress term premia and sustain mortgage/credit functioning. Housing demand is a partial bright spot, but tighter underwriting tempers the boost.

Net tone: cautious with downside risks, now tilted more negative given the SLOOS evidence of tighter bank credit supply and weaker demand, partially offset by credible policy backstops.
